title: PostgreSQL DBA Part 25: Find Slow Queries with pg_stat_statements
description: Enable pg_stat_statements on PostgreSQL 18, find the queries that cost the most time and I/O, and prove a fix by resetting one statement. Real output.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 17 release notes (column renames, reset return value)

reviewNotes:
Series part 25. Publish Part 24 first (Parts 19-24 are not live yet; Part 24 is named without a link and is not in related). TEST ENVIRONMENT: PostgreSQL 18 could NOT be run in this sandbox. postgresql-18 (18.7-1.pgdg24.04+5) is available from PGDG but depends on liburing2 from the Ubuntu archive, which the sandbox network blocks (apt: "Depends: liburing2 (>= 2.5) but it is not installable"). Following the task instructions, all SQL and shell examples were run on the distribution PostgreSQL 16.15 (Ubuntu 16.15-0ubuntu0.24.04.1) on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, cluster 16 main, port 5432, pgbench 16.15. The article is written for PostgreSQL 18 (paths /etc/postgresql/18/main, postgresql@18-main, /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin). Documentation followed: PostgreSQL 18 docs (/docs/18/; postgresql.org/docs/current now shows 19) plus the 17 and 18 release notes.
Every column queried (queryid, query, calls, total_exec_time, mean/stddev/max_exec_time, rows, shared_blks_hit/read, temp_blks_written, userid) exists in both 16 and 18 with the same meaning, so the result tables are real 16 output. Items that differ on 18 and are captioned '(expected output)' or described in text only: (1) pg_stat_statements_reset() returns timestamptz since 17 (void on 16), so its output is described in words, not shown; (2) the IN-list grouping example output is the 18 behaviour from the docs (on 16 it really printed separate rows 'IN ($1, $2, $3)' and 'IN ($1, $2, $3, $4)', both calls 1, plus '= $1' calls 2); (3) pg_lsclusters for 18 main; (4) the 'must be loaded via "shared_preload_libraries"' error: on 16 the real text is unquoted ('must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries'); I wrote the quoted form assuming the PostgreSQL 17 change that quotes GUC names in messages, PLEASE VERIFY on 18; (5) the reload log lines are real 16 lines with the path changed to 18 and timestamps removed; (6) the EXPLAIN plan is real 16 output, trimmed, with a sentence saying 18 shows fractional rows (rows=5.67). Not run: track_io_timing read-time columns (shared_blk_read_time is 17+; on 16 it is blk_read_time), 18-only columns parallel_workers_to_launch/launched, wal_buffers_full. Step 2 'before' lines are simplified (comments trimmed). Sandbox has no systemd, so restarts were done with pg_ctlcluster; the article shows systemctl restart postgresql@18-main with pg_ctlcluster as the alternative. Step 15 used SET ROLE as postgres instead of logging in as the roles (peer auth). pgbench and timing numbers are real from this sandbox and will differ on other hardware; the article says so. GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_stat_statements_reset TO monitor (no argument list) was tested on 16 and lets the role reset. Please re-run Steps 1-4, 7 and the IN-list example on a real PostgreSQL 18 server before publishing.

data.text: This is Part 25 of the PostgreSQL DBA series. In Part 24 we used the cumulative statistics views to see which tables and indexes are busy. Those views tell you where the work happens, but not which SQL statements cause it. That is the job of pg_stat_statements, and by the end of this part you will have it running on PostgreSQL 18 and know how to read it to find the queries worth fixing first.

pg_stat_statements is an extension that ships with PostgreSQL. Once it is loaded, it keeps a running total for every distinct SQL statement the server executes: how many times it ran, the total and average time, how many rows it returned and how many data blocks it touched. You then query it like a normal view and sort by the column that matters to you.

Turning it on takes one configuration line, one restart and one SQL command. The rest of this part is about reading the numbers correctly, because the slowest single query is often not the query that costs your server the most.
What you will learn

items.content: How pg_stat_statements groups statements and why you see $1 instead of real values
How to enable it on Ubuntu: shared_preload_libraries, a restart and CREATE EXTENSION
Four queries that find the most expensive SQL: by total time, by average time, by share of the workload and by I/O
How to prove a fix worked by resetting the statistics for one statement
Who can see other users' query text, and how to grant it with pg_read_all_stats
The settings that control the extension and the mistakes that stop it working

data.text: Prerequisites

items.content: Parts 1 to 24 of this series, especially Part 5 (editing postgresql.conf, reload versus restart), Part 7 (roles and privileges) and Part 24 (statistics views).
One Ubuntu server with PostgreSQL 18 from the PGDG repository and the default cluster 18 main on port 5432, set up as in Part 2.
A user with sudo rights. You run SQL as the postgres operating system user, which connects as the postgres superuser through peer authentication.
Permission to restart PostgreSQL once. Loading pg_stat_statements cannot be done with a reload, so plan the restart for a quiet moment on a production server.

data.text: How it works

Think of pg_stat_statements as a till receipt for your database. Every time a statement finishes, the extension adds a line to the receipt for that kind of statement: one more call, so many milliseconds, so many rows. It never stores every single execution; it only keeps running totals per statement.

To decide which statements are "the same kind", PostgreSQL calculates a query identifier (the queryid column), a hash of the statement's structure after parsing. Two statements that differ only in their constant values get the same identifier. So WHERE customer_id = 42 and WHERE customer_id = 7 land on one line, and the extension shows the constant as a placeholder: WHERE customer_id = $1. This is called normalisation.

The query identifier is computed by the core server when the setting compute_query_id allows it. Its default, auto, lets modules such as pg_stat_statements switch it on automatically, so you normally do not touch it.

The counters live in shared memory, the memory area every PostgreSQL process can read. Shared memory is sized when the server starts, which is why the module must be listed in shared_preload_libraries and why adding or removing it needs a restart. The query texts themselves are kept in a file on disk (in the pg_stat_tmp folder of the data directory), not in shared memory.

Statistics are collected for all databases in the cluster. The CREATE EXTENSION command only creates the view and functions in the database where you run it, so you can read the numbers. Each row of the view is one combination of user, database, query identifier and whether the statement was top level.

data.code:
application sessions --(SQL)--> backend process --(when the statement ends)--> counters in shared memory
                                                                              |
DBA: SELECT ... FROM pg_stat_statements  <-------------------------------------+
data.caption: Where the numbers come from

data.text: The columns you will use most often:

content: Hash that identifies the normalised statement
Text of a representative statement, with constants replaced by $1, $2 ...
Number of times the statement was executed
Total time spent executing it, in milliseconds
Average, slowest and spread of execution time, in milliseconds
8 kB blocks found in shared buffers / read from outside them
Blocks written to temporary files, for example by sorts that did not fit in work_mem
True if the client issued the statement directly, false if it ran inside a function

data.text: Times are in milliseconds and cover the execution phase only. Planning time is in separate *_plan_time columns, which stay at zero unless you turn on pg_stat_statements.track_planning.
Enable pg_stat_statements
Step 1: Check whether it is already loaded
On the database server (db1), as a sudo user. First see what shared_preload_libraries contains now, so you do not remove another library that is already there.

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW shared_preload_libraries;"

shared_preload_libraries 
--------------------------
 
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The value is empty, which is the default. If your server already lists libraries here (for example auto_explain from Part 23), keep them and add pg_stat_statements to the list, separated by a comma.
Step 2: Add the library to postgresql.conf
On db1, as a sudo user. Open the main configuration file in an editor:

data.code: sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

data.text: Find the two lines below and change them. track_io_timing is optional but useful: it fills in the read and write time columns so you can see how long a statement waited for disk.

data.code:
# before
#shared_preload_libraries = ''
#track_io_timing = off

# after
shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements'
track_io_timing = on
data.caption: /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

content: Server start only: needs a restart
Reload; only superusers and users with the SET privilege can change it in a session
Leave it at auto; pg_stat_statements enables it

data.text: The documentation warns that track_io_timing asks the operating system for the current time over and over, which can be expensive on some platforms. Measure the overhead with /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_test_timing before enabling it on a busy production server.
To see what happens if you only reload, run a reload now and check the pending_restart flag:

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT pg_reload_conf();"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT name, setting, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('shared_preload_libraries','track_io_timing');"

name           | setting | pending_restart 
--------------------------+---------+-----------------
 shared_preload_libraries |         | t
 track_io_timing          | on      | f
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: track_io_timing is already active because it is reloadable. shared_preload_libraries is still empty and pending_restart is t: the new value is waiting for a restart. The server log says the same:

data.code:
LOG:  parameter "track_io_timing" changed to "on"
LOG:  parameter "shared_preload_libraries" cannot be changed without restarting the server
LOG:  configuration file "/etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf" contains errors; unaffected changes were applied
data.caption: Output from /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log (timestamps removed)

data.text: Step 3: Restart the cluster
On db1, as a sudo user. A restart disconnects every session, so tell application owners first.

data.code:
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main
pg_lsclusters

Ver Cluster Port Status Owner    Data directory              Log file
18  main    5432 online postgres /var/lib/postgresql/18/main /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: If you prefer the PostgreSQL wrapper, sudo pg_ctlcluster 18 main restart does the same thing. Verify that the library is now loaded and look at the extension's own settings:

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW shared_preload_libraries;"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT name, setting, context FROM pg_settings WHERE name LIKE 'pg_stat_statements.%' ORDER BY name;"

shared_preload_libraries 
--------------------------
 pg_stat_statements
(1 row)

               name                | setting |  context   
-----------------------------------+---------+------------
 pg_stat_statements.max            | 5000    | postmaster
 pg_stat_statements.save           | on      | sighup
 pg_stat_statements.track          | top     | superuser
 pg_stat_statements.track_planning | off     | superuser
 pg_stat_statements.track_utility  | on      | superuser
(5 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The context column tells you how each setting is changed: postmaster means restart, sighup means reload, superuser means a superuser can also change it in a session. These defaults match the documentation and are fine to start with.
Step 4: Create the extension in your working database

On db1, as the postgres user. We use a scratch database called shopdb. Create the extension in every database from which you want to read the statistics; it still records statements from all databases.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE DATABASE shopdb;"
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements;"

CREATE DATABASE
CREATE EXTENSION
data.caption: Output

data.text: Verify with the extension's information view, which has a single row:

data.code: SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements_info;

data.text: dealloc counts how many times entries were thrown away because more than pg_stat_statements.max distinct statements were seen. stats_reset is when all statistics were last cleared. If you see this row, the extension is working.

Many DBAs also create the extension in the postgres database, because that is where they connect for admin work. To undo everything later: DROP EXTENSION pg_stat_statements; in each database, remove it from shared_preload_libraries and restart.
Create a sample workload
Statistics are only interesting when something runs. We build an orders table and drive four kinds of statements against it with pgbench, the benchmarking tool that comes with PostgreSQL.
Step 5: Create the sample table
On db1, as the postgres user, in shopdb. The table has a primary key on order_id but, on purpose, no index on customer_id.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id  integer       NOT NULL,
    status       text          NOT NULL,
    amount       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    note         text,
    created_at   timestamptz   NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, status, amount, note, created_at)
SELECT (random() * 20000)::int + 1,
       (ARRAY['new','paid','shipped'])[1 + (g % 3)],
       round((random() * 5000)::numeric, 2),
       md5(g::text) || md5((g * 7)::text),
       now() - (g || ' minutes')::interval
  FROM generate_series(1, 300000) AS g;

ANALYZE orders;
data.caption: 300,000 sample orders

data.code:
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 300000
ANALYZE
data.caption: Output

data.text: Step 6: Write four workload scripts
On db1, as the postgres operating system user (its home directory is /var/lib/postgresql). Each file is one pgbench transaction. \set picks a random value, and :cid or :oid inserts it into the SQL.

data.code:
sudo -i -u postgres
mkdir -p ~/workload && cd ~/workload

cat > by_customer.sql <<'EOF'
\set cid random(1, 20000)
SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = :cid;
EOF

cat > by_id.sql <<'EOF'
\set oid random(1, 300000)
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE order_id = :oid;
EOF

cat > ship.sql <<'EOF'
\set oid random(1, 300000)
UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE order_id = :oid;
EOF

cat > report.sql <<'EOF'
SELECT order_id, note FROM orders ORDER BY note LIMIT 50000;
EOF

data.text: There is no output. Check with ls ~/workload; you should see the four .sql files.
Step 7: Reset the statistics and run the workload
Still as the postgres user. Start from a clean slate so the numbers only describe this test, then run all four scripts together for 30 seconds.

data.code:
psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();"

/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pgbench -n -c 4 -j 2 -T 30 \
  -f by_customer.sql@2 -f by_id.sql@20 -f ship.sql@5 -f report.sql@1 shopdb

content: Perform no vacuuming before running the test; needed for a custom test without the standard pgbench tables
Number of clients simulated, that is, number of concurrent database sessions
Number of worker threads within pgbench
Run the test for this many seconds
Add a transaction script read from the file; the weight sets how often it is picked relative to the others

data.code:
transaction type: multiple scripts
scaling factor: 1
query mode: simple
number of clients: 4
number of threads: 2
maximum number of tries: 1
duration: 30 s
number of transactions actually processed: 11428
number of failed transactions: 0 (0.000%)
latency average = 10.538 ms
initial connection time = 6.115 ms
tps = 379.562821 (without initial connection time)
data.caption: Output (pgbench summary, per-script lines trimmed)

data.text: On PostgreSQL 18 the reset prints one row containing the time of the reset (a timestamp with time zone); before PostgreSQL 17 the function returned nothing. The pgbench numbers depend on your hardware, so yours will differ. What matters is that 11,428 transactions ran with no failures, and now pg_stat_statements has something to show.
Find the most expensive queries
There is no single "slowest query". A DBA looks at the same view from four angles, and each answers a different question.
Step 8: Sort by total execution time
On db1, as the postgres user, in shopdb. This is the most useful query: which statements consumed the most server time overall?

data.code:
SELECT queryid,
       left(query, 60)                    AS query,
       calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)  AS mean_ms,
       rows
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
 LIMIT 5;
data.caption: Top 5 statements by total time

data.code:
queryid        |                            query                             | calls | total_ms | mean_ms |   rows   
----------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+-------+----------+---------+----------
 -5259757585030337844 | SELECT order_id, note FROM orders ORDER BY note LIMIT $1     |   415 |    90482 |  218.03 | 20750000
  8050982999726607845 | SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE customer_i |   790 |    18146 |   22.97 |    11862
  6255225213605425321 | SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE order |  8217 |      115 |    0.01 |     8217
 -8472490887429388584 | UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE order_id = $2            |  2006 |       96 |    0.05 |     2006
  3042479536081193248 | SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset()                            |     1 |        0 |    0.07 |        1
(5 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Read it row by row. The report query ran only 415 times but used about 90 seconds of execution time, because each run takes about 218 ms. The customer lookup comes second: 790 calls at about 23 ms each. The lookup by primary key ran 8,217 times, ten times more often, yet used only 115 ms in total.

Notice the placeholders. pgbench sent thousands of different customer_id values, but you see one row with $1. The queryid is the stable handle you use to refer to that row later. The total of 90,482 ms is larger than the 30 seconds of the test because four sessions worked in parallel.
The query text is shortened with left(query, 60) only to fit the screen. Remove left() or use \x in psql to see the full text.
Step 9: See each statement's share of the workload
A percentage is easier to explain to a manager or developer than milliseconds. The window function sum() OVER () adds up the total time of all rows.

data.code:
SELECT left(query, 45) AS query,
       calls,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms,
       round((100 * total_exec_time /
              sum(total_exec_time) OVER ())::numeric, 1) AS pct_of_total
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
 LIMIT 4;

query                     | calls | total_ms | pct_of_total 
-----------------------------------------------+-------+----------+--------------
 SELECT order_id, note FROM orders ORDER BY no |   415 |    90482 |         83.1
 SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders W |   790 |    18146 |         16.7
 SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM ord |  8217 |      115 |          0.1
 UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE order_id  |  2006 |       96 |          0.1
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Two statements account for almost 100% of the execution time. Tuning the other two would save almost nothing, however often they run. On a real server this pattern is common: a handful of statements cause most of the load, and this query tells you which ones.
Step 10: Sort by average time
Average time finds statements that feel slow to a user, even if they run rarely. The filter calls >= 50 hides one-off commands such as an index build.

data.code:
SELECT left(query, 50)                     AS query,
       calls,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)   AS mean_ms,
       round(stddev_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS stddev_ms,
       round(max_exec_time::numeric, 2)    AS max_ms
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 WHERE calls >= 50
 ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
 LIMIT 5;

query                        | calls | mean_ms | stddev_ms | max_ms 
----------------------------------------------------+-------+---------+-----------+--------
 SELECT order_id, note FROM orders ORDER BY note LI |   415 |  218.03 |     34.24 | 315.48
 SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE  |   790 |   22.97 |      6.34 |   61.31
 UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE order_id = $2  |  2006 |    0.05 |      0.16 |   4.31
 SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM orders W |  8217 |    0.01 |      0.06 |   5.22
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The standard deviation (stddev_ms) shows how much each run varies. A small average with a large maximum, like the UPDATE (0.05 ms average, 4.31 ms maximum), usually means the statement sometimes waited, for example for a lock or for disk. A consistently slow statement, like the report, has a high average and a modest spread.
Step 11: Sort by I/O
Time depends on how busy the server was. Block counts do not, so they are a fairer way to compare the work a statement does.

data.code:
SELECT left(query, 45)                           AS query,
       shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read        AS blocks_touched,
       round(100.0 * shared_blks_hit /
             nullif(shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read, 0), 1) AS hit_pct,
       temp_blks_written
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 ORDER BY shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read DESC
 LIMIT 4;

query                     | blocks_touched | hit_pct | temp_blks_written 
-----------------------------------------------+----------------+---------+-------------------
 SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders W |        3790420 |    97.9 |                 0
 SELECT order_id, note FROM orders ORDER BY no |        2033692 |    98.5 |           1269757
 SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM ord |          32916 |    97.4 |                 0
 UPDATE orders SET status = $1 WHERE order_id  |          22880 |    99.0 |                 0
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Now the customer lookup is first: 3,790,420 blocks for 790 calls is about 4,800 blocks (around 37 MB) per call to return about 15 rows. That is the signature of a full table scan. hit_pct is the share of blocks found in shared buffers, the PostgreSQL cache from Part 1.

The report query wrote 1,269,757 temporary blocks: its sort did not fit in work_mem and spilled to disk. That is a memory tuning question for Part 28. nullif(..., 0) avoids a division by zero for statements that touch no blocks.

With track_io_timing = on, the columns shared_blk_read_time and shared_blk_write_time show how many milliseconds each statement spent on disk reads and writes. Before PostgreSQL 17 these columns were called blk_read_time and blk_write_time, so older monitoring queries may need updating.
Fix one query and prove it
Finding a slow statement is half the work. The other half is showing that your change helped. pg_stat_statements lets you reset the counters for one statement and measure again.
Step 12: Confirm the cause
On db1, in shopdb. Take the full text of the statement, put a real value in place of $1, and look at the plan (Part 26 covers reading plans in depth):

data.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT order_id, amount, status FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 4242;

Gather  (...) (actual time=0.418..15.027 rows=17 loops=1)
  Workers Planned: 2
  Workers Launched: 2
  Buffers: shared hit=4798
  ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (...)
        Filter: (customer_id = 4242)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 99994
        Buffers: shared hit=4798
Execution Time: 15.084 ms
data.caption: Output (trimmed)

data.text: A Parallel Seq Scan reads the whole table and throws away almost every row to return 17. That matches the 4,800 blocks per call we saw in Step 11. On PostgreSQL 18 the row counts in this output are shown with two decimals, for example rows=5.67, because they are averaged across loops.
Step 13: Add the index and reset only this statement
Create the missing index, then clear the counters for this one queryid. The function's arguments are user id, database id and query id; 0 means "any".

data.code:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);

SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(0, 0, 8050982999726607845);
CREATE INDEX
data.caption: Output of the first statement

data.text: The reset returns one row with the reset time, as in Step 7. Your queryid will be different from the one shown here; copy it from your own Step 8 output. Only this statement's row is cleared. The other rows and the stats_reset time in pg_stat_statements_info stay as they were, because that time only changes when all statistics are reset.
On a busy production server, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so that writes to the table are not blocked while the index builds. The plain form here is fine on a test server.
Step 14: Run the workload again and compare
As the postgres user, in ~/workload, run the same pgbench command as Step 7 (without the reset), then look at the statement by its queryid:

data.code:
/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pgbench -n -c 4 -j 2 -T 30 \
  -f by_customer.sql@2 -f by_id.sql@20 -f ship.sql@5 -f report.sql@1 shopdb

psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT left(query, 50) AS query, calls,
       round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
       shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read AS blocks_touched
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 WHERE queryid = 8050982999726607845;"

data.text: The same statement now reads about 18 blocks instead of about 4,800 and runs hundreds of times faster. The queryid stayed the same, because creating an index does not change the statement's structure. That is what makes before-and-after comparisons with pg_stat_statements so easy.
Control who can see query text

Query text can contain sensitive values, so the documentation limits it: only superusers and roles with the privileges of the built-in role pg_read_all_stats can see the text and queryid of statements run by other users. Everyone else still sees the numbers.
Step 15: Give a monitoring role read access

On db1, as the postgres user, in shopdb. We create an application role and a monitoring role. SET ROLE lets the superuser act as each of them without setting up passwords (roles were covered in Part 7).

data.code:
username |          query           | calls 
----------+--------------------------+-------
 app_user | <insufficient privilege> |     1
 app_user | <insufficient privilege> |     1
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output of the last SELECT

data.text: The monitor role sees that app_user ran statements, but not what they were. (The filter on SET% cannot hide rows whose text is hidden, so the SET ROLE command appears too.) Now grant the built-in role and try again:

data.code:
username |                     query                     | calls 
----------+-----------------------------------------------+-------
 app_user | SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = $1 |     1
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The text is visible now. Note that pg_read_all_stats does not allow resetting: by default only superusers can run pg_stat_statements_reset. To let the monitor role reset too, grant it explicitly with GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_stat_statements_reset TO monitor;. To undo this step: REVOKE pg_read_all_stats FROM monitor; then DROP ROLE monitor; and DROP ROLE app_user; (revoke the SELECT grant on orders first).
Settings and PostgreSQL 18 changes
How statements are grouped

Statements that differ only in constants, letter case or spacing are merged, and the stored text is the first one seen. On PostgreSQL 18, IN lists of different lengths are also merged into one entry, shown with a comment marker. Run this in shopdb:

data.code:
query                          | calls 
--------------------------------------------------------+-------
 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = $1               |     2
 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id IN ($1 /*, ... */) |     2
(2 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output on PostgreSQL 18)

data.text: The two = $1 statements merged even though one was lower case with extra spaces. Before PostgreSQL 18, each IN list length got its own row (IN ($1, $2, $3) and IN ($1, $2, $3, $4)), which could fill the view with near-duplicates from applications that build IN lists of varying size.

Other PostgreSQL 18 changes for this extension: the new columns parallel_workers_to_launch, parallel_workers_launched and wal_buffers_full; CREATE TABLE AS and DECLARE statements are now tracked; and constants in SET commands are replaced by placeholders, so many different SET values no longer create separate rows.
The configuration parameters

content: Maximum number of statements tracked; the least-executed are discarded beyond this. Restart needed
top: statements sent by clients; all: also statements inside functions; none: off
Whether commands other than SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE are tracked
Whether planning time is tracked; the documentation warns of a noticeable performance penalty under high concurrency
Whether statistics are kept across server shutdowns. Reload

data.text: If dealloc in pg_stat_statements_info keeps rising, the view is too small for your workload and entries are being thrown away. Raise pg_stat_statements.max (for example to 10000) and restart. The extra shared memory is proportional to this value and is used whenever the module is loaded, even with track = none.
Common mistakes and how to fix them
ERROR: pg_stat_statements must be loaded via shared_preload_libraries
CREATE EXTENSION succeeds even when the library is not preloaded, but the first query fails:

data.code: ERROR:  pg_stat_statements must be loaded via "shared_preload_libraries"
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Fix: add the library to shared_preload_libraries (Step 2) and restart. A reload is not enough; check pending_restart in pg_settings as shown in Step 2.
ERROR: relation "pg_stat_statements" does not exist

data.caption: Output

data.text: You are connected to a database where the extension was not created (here, the postgres database). Fix: run CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements; in that database, or connect to one that has it. If the extension lives in a schema that is not in your search_path (Part 8), qualify the name, for example public.pg_stat_statements.
Query text shows <insufficient privilege>
The role you are using is not a superuser and lacks pg_read_all_stats. Fix: GRANT pg_read_all_stats TO monitor; as in Step 15.
ERROR: permission denied for function pg_stat_statements_reset

data.code: ERROR:  permission denied for function pg_stat_statements_reset
data.caption: Output

data.text: Reading and resetting are separate privileges. Fix: reset as a superuser, or grant EXECUTE on the function to the role that needs it.
Sorting only by mean time

A 2-second report that runs once a night looks worse than a 20 ms query that runs a million times a day, but the second one costs far more. Always look at total_exec_time first (Step 8), then at averages.
The query column is empty (NULL)

The documentation explains that if the external file of query texts grows too large, the extension may discard all texts; the statistics stay but query shows NULL. If this happens, consider reducing pg_stat_statements.max to prevent it recurring. Applications that generate very long or unique SQL texts make this more likely.
Expecting queryid to survive an upgrade

The documentation says it is not safe to assume queryid stays the same across major versions, and it can change if a referenced object is dropped and recreated. Save query text along with the identifier when you keep history.
Practice exercise

items.content: Using the workload from Step 7, add a fifth script that runs SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = :s; with a random status. Run pgbench again and find its rank by total time and by blocks touched.
Write one query that lists the top 3 statements by temp_blks_written, showing calls and temp_blks_written / calls per call.

data.title: Answers
data.text: Answer for task 2: SELECT left(query, 45) AS query, calls, temp_blks_written, temp_blks_written / calls AS temp_per_call FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE temp_blks_written > 0 ORDER BY temp_blks_written DESC LIMIT 3; On our test server only the report query appears, with about 3,060 temporary blocks per call (1,269,757 / 415). For task 1, there is no index on status, so every call reads the whole table: expect it near the top by blocks touched, with roughly the same blocks per call as the customer lookup had before its index.
Quick reference

data.code:
# 1. Check what is preloaded now
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW shared_preload_libraries;"

# 2. Edit the config: shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_stat_statements', track_io_timing = on
sudo nano /etc/postgresql/18/main/postgresql.conf

# 3. Restart (a reload is not enough) and verify
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW shared_preload_libraries;"

# 4. Create the extension in the database you read from
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements;"
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT * FROM pg_stat_statements_info;"

# 5. Clear all statistics before a test
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();"

# 6. Generate load with custom scripts (as postgres, in ~/workload)
/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pgbench -n -c 4 -j 2 -T 30 -f by_customer.sql@2 -f by_id.sql@20 -f ship.sql@5 -f report.sql@1 shopdb

# 7. Top statements by total time
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT queryid, left(query, 60) AS query, calls, round(total_exec_time::numeric, 0) AS total_ms, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 5;"

# 8. Reset one statement after a fix (use your own queryid)
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset(0, 0, 8050982999726607845);"

# 9. Let a monitoring role read other users' query text
sudo -u postgres psql -d shopdb -c "GRANT pg_read_all_stats TO monitor;"

data.text: Summary and what's next

items.content: pg_stat_statements keeps running totals per normalised statement for the whole cluster
It needs shared_preload_libraries plus a restart, then CREATE EXTENSION in each database you read from
Sort by total_exec_time first, then look at mean time, share of the workload and blocks touched
Use temp_blks_written to spot sorts and hashes that spill to disk
Prove a fix with pg_stat_statements_reset(0, 0, queryid) and a second measurement
Grant pg_read_all_stats to monitoring roles; resetting needs a separate grant
Watch dealloc in pg_stat_statements_info and raise pg_stat_statements.max if it grows

data.text: In Part 26 we take the statements you found here and read their execution plans with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), the way a DBA does.

linkedin.post:
Your slowest query is often not the one hurting your PostgreSQL server the most.

In a 30-second test, a lookup by primary key ran 8,217 times and used 115 ms in total. A customer lookup ran only 790 times but used 18 seconds, because it scanned the whole table every time.

pg_stat_statements shows you this in one query. What to know:

→ Add it to shared_preload_libraries and restart. A reload is not enough.
→ Run CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements in the database you query from. It still records all databases.
→ Sort by total_exec_time first, not by mean time. Total time is what your server actually pays.
→ Check shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read per call. Thousands of blocks for a handful of rows means a missing index.
→ After a fix, reset one statement with pg_stat_statements_reset(0, 0, queryid) and measure again.

On PostgreSQL 18, IN lists of different lengths are finally merged into one entry.

This is Part 25 of my PostgreSQL DBA series. Follow along for the next part on EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).

slides.title: Find slow queries with pg_stat_statements
slides.body: PostgreSQL DBA series, Part 25: enable it, read it, prove your fix

slides.title: Step 1: load it and restart
points: Add it to shared_preload_libraries in postgresql.conf
A reload is not enough: restart postgresql@18-main
Then CREATE EXTENSION in the database you query from

slides.title: Step 2: sort by total time
slides.code:
SELECT left(query, 40) AS query,
  calls,
  round(total_exec_time::numeric)
    AS total_ms,
  round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2)
    AS mean_ms
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;
points: Total time is what the server pays; mean time can mislead

slides.title: Step 3: look at blocks per call
points: About 4,800 blocks per call for 15 rows meant a full table scan
temp_blks_written shows sorts spilling to disk

slides.title: Step 4: fix and prove it
points: Mean time fell from 22.97 ms to 0.05 ms in our test

slides.title: Access and PostgreSQL 18
points: Other users' query text needs pg_read_all_stats
Resetting needs its own EXECUTE grant
PostgreSQL 18 merges IN lists of any length into one row
